title: The ssh noticer starts stopped WSL distros: it picks distros from the cached running flag and runs wsl.exe -d <distro> in each
scenario: Setup: WSL is on, and Ember read the facts while Ubuntu was running (at startup, refreshWsl sets wslFacts.distros[Ubuntu].running = true). The user closes their WSL tab and Ubuntu stops. With no WSLg window on screen, nothing reads the running set again: the router returns before facts() and the picker isn't opened, so wslFacts keeps running:true indefinitely. The user then runs `ssh deploy@build-01` in Windows Terminal. Because the title looks like ssh, noticer.check() runs. The wsl() closure (runtime.ts:943-947) passes distros:["Ubuntu"] from the stale flag, and userSshProcessesWith (notice-ssh.ts:316-321) runs `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu --exec /bin/sh -s`, which boots Ubuntu. Nothing checks runningNow(), and the probe is not under the job host. It happens again on every later check (title changes at least 10 s apart), each time after WSL has idled the distro back down. I reproduced it with the targets-runtime rig: wsl.runningNow() returned an empty set, the noticer still passed {wsl:{distros:["Ubuntu"]}}, and the real reader spawned ["C:\\Program Files\\WSL\\wsl.exe","-d","Ubuntu","--exec","/bin/sh","-s"]. This is a distro started by Ember without the user asking.
fix: Choose the distros from an uncached read (await wsl.runningNow()) right before reading, or run the reader through WslRunner.runScript without mayBoot, which re-checks runningNow() and runs under the job host. Do not use wslFacts.running for anything that spawns wsl.exe.

title: GWSL's X server windows are not treated as remote surfaces, so Ember can act in them and they are not masked
scenario: GWSL draws Linux apps through its bundled VcXsrv, whose program image is GWSL_vcxsrv.exe (or GWSL_vcxsrv_lowdpi.exe). The Windows backend names the window's app "GWSL_vcxsrv" (names.ts programName), and REMOTE_SURFACE.win32 / WINDOWS_X_SERVER only match the exact name `gwsl(.exe)`. The WSL doctor already expects this name: X_SERVERS uses /^gwsl.*\.exe$/ and reports "GWSL" for GWSL_vcxsrv.exe. Checked: isRemoteSurface("GWSL_vcxsrv","win32") is false, while "vcxsrv" is true. PolicyEngine.decide({kind:"keys", app:"GWSL_vcxsrv", window:"ana@pc: ~"}) returns confirm, where vcxsrv returns never. As a result, a Linux terminal, polkit or pinentry window shown by GWSL can be typed or clicked into through the borrowed keyboard and mouse after a single confirm. One grant on GWSL_vcxsrv covers every Linux app it shows, the same-process pointer check accepts any of its windows, and its windows are not blacked out in screenshots.
fix: Match GWSL's real image names in both regexes, for example `gwsl(?:_vcxsrv(?:_lowdpi)?)?`, or reuse the doctor's gwsl.* rule, so REMOTE_SURFACE, isWindowsXServer and the doctor agree. Add a test for "GWSL_vcxsrv".

title: A stale isRunning() permanently assigns a newly started distro's msrdc to another distro, so its Linux windows are never identified
scenario: Ubuntu is running and Debian is stopped. The user asks "open gedit in Debian". launchWslg reads wsl.facts(), which is cached and does not refresh the running set, and then opens the .lnk; Debian boots and its msrdc (a new pid) shows gedit. The worker's first look() calls wsl.isRunning("Debian"), which returns the cached set (still stopped) and only starts a background refresh. So candidates=[Ubuntu] and showing=1, and line 327 maps Debian's msrdc pid to "Ubuntu". The mapping is only dropped when that msrdc exits or Ubuntu stops being a candidate, so it never corrects. Debian's windows are matched against Ubuntu's frames, no Debian helper is ever started, and the app Ember just opened stays "msrdc" (refused and masked) while Ubuntu runs. Reproduced with the router fakes: with isRunning("Debian") false on the first look and true on five later looks, the snapshot never contains hwnd 21 and helpers were created only for ["Ubuntu"]. In the control run, without the lag, 21 is identified as wsl:Debian:gedit.
fix: Before using the single-running-distro shortcut, read the running set uncached (runningNow()), or don't cache an assignment made by that shortcut. Re-check pidDistro whenever the number of running WSL 2 distros grows.

title: A WSLg shortcut whose Linux command starts with VAR=value passes the terminal check, so Ember opens a terminal
scenario: The shortcut is `wslg.exe -d Ubuntu --cd "~" -- GDK_BACKEND=x11 gnome-terminal`. Such a shortcut can come from a user-writable .desktop file in the distro, which is the threat critique wsl-23 names. TOKEN allows '=', so wslgLaunch accepts argv ["GDK_BACKEND=x11","gnome-terminal"]. The distro's shell reads the first word as an assignment and starts gnome-terminal. linuxTerminal() calls isTerminalApp({argv}, "linux"), which treats "gdk_backend=x11" as the program, so the answer is not a terminal (the same command written with `env` is detected). Verified: isTerminalApp returned false, and launch() spawned explorer.exe with the .lnk. The same check is at line 180 in launchWslg. Ember opens a terminal (or `X=1 bash`), breaking 'Ember never opens terminals'.
fix: Judge the Linux command as the shell will run it: skip leading NAME=value words (for example call linuxTerminal with ["env", ...p.argv]), or reject an assignment word in command position in wslgLaunch.

title: Apps of a running root distro are launched because the root check only uses a uid learned from commands
scenario: Example: an imported distro whose default user is root is running, and no Ember command has run there yet. WslDistro.defaultUid is filled only by learnedUid() from a command runner's facts. The router learns uid 0 from the helper's status, but only sets st.problem="root" and does not feed the uid back into the facts. So facts.defaultUid is null and wslgRefusal returns null. launchWslg never asks WslService.defaultUid(), which exists to read the uid of a running distro without booting it. fix: In launchWslg, when the target distro is running and defaultUid is null, await wsl.defaultUid(distro) (it never boots) and refuse on 0. Alternatively, have the router record a helper's uid 0 in the service's uid map.

title: No window system and commands off: show_me reports a guide started that fails at once, and the conductor gets three extra tools
scenario: Linux session where X11 can't be opened (wsSeen is null, so main passes hands=undefined). There is no SSH host, commands are off, and optionally an admin policy without the new keys (R5: commands off). Main always passes targets and taskBase, so the TaskManager is now created (host.ts:817, `hands || targets`). Effects: (a) the conductor's tools grow from 4 to 7 (list_tasks, cancel_task, steer_task), so the tool list is not the same as base; (b) show_me (host.ts:977-996) never asks handsFor. It returns "Guide … started: Ember will point at each step… Tell the user to follow Ember", then makeWorker gets a refusal and the guide card fails at once with the model-directed sentence "Ember can't use this computer's screen here, and commands are off. Tell the user they can turn commands on in Ember's settings." (runtime.ts:1091). That sentence is shown and announced to the user as the task result. (c) start_task returns the same sentence, which tells the user to turn commands on even when the admin policy forbids it. At base, start_task said "Ember cannot operate applications in this session (no desktop access)…" and show_me said "Ember can't point at things in this session (no desktop access)…", with no task. Reproduced with AgentHost plus buildTargets({hands:null}): TOOLS had 7 entries, SHOW_ME said "Guide 1-… started", and TASKS showed it failed with that summary.
fix: In show_me, refuse before queueing when the bound target has no screen (handsFor(...) not ok, or binding.desktop !== "screen"), using base's text. Create the TaskManager, and so the task tools, only when hands exist or some target can actually take a task (desktop or live commands). In handsFor/registry, use wording that depends on commandMode, and don't say "the user can turn commands on" when the admin mode is off.

title: "Starting Ubuntu…" never reaches the command window: the distro boots in the facts read, before any tab exists
